summary: A tutorial for people running gateways between X.400 and Internet mail, written to help new gateway managers understand the complicated rules of RFC 1327.

plainLanguage.summary: Two post offices use different rules. This is a beginner guide for the person who runs the desk that passes letters between them.

questions: x.400 to internet mail gateway tutorial
how to run an x.400 gateway
how do address mappings work in email gateways
subtitle: How to translate mail between X.400 and Internet standards using RFC 1327 mapping rules

tldr.problem: X.400 and Internet mail systems had different address formats, message structures, and protocols, so messages crossing gateways became unreadable and replies could not route back correctly unless all gateways used identical mapping rules.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1327 defines a standard set of address mappings (default encoding and exception tables) that all gateways must follow, along with rules for mapping message service elements (like subject, recipients) and a coordination service to distribute consistent mapping tables worldwide.
tldr.outcome: Gateway managers can implement X.400/Internet mail interworking consistently, though the process remains complex because the two address spaces are fundamentally different.

today: RFC 1506 remains a historical record of X.400/SMTP gateway implementation published in 1993. X.400 mail systems largely disappeared from production use as SMTP and POP/IMAP became dominant. The coordination mechanisms and global mapping tables described here influenced later email standardization efforts.

sections.title: The Two Mail Worlds
sections.content:
The Internet mail world developed from ARPA research, using RFC 822 message format and SMTP protocol. In Europe, where earlier systems were not in place, X.400 (an OSI standard) became the de facto mail system. By the early 1990s, both systems coexisted, and a message from an X.400 user often needed to reach an Internet mail user, and vice versa.

Early gateways each implemented mappings differently: they translated addresses and message headers in various ways. When a message crossed two gateways, recipients saw corrupted sender addresses. When an X.400 user replied to an Internet mail user who had sent through a gateway, the reply might get routed back through a different gateway, leading to mismatched addresses that made the conversation unintelligible.

RFC 1327 was created to define a single global standard for all these mappings. Every gateway must follow the same rules so that messages can reliably cross any number of gateways and still be understood.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet used one mail system, Europe used another. Mail between them kept getting scrambled because each gateway translated addresses differently. RFC 1327 says everyone must translate the same way.

sections.title: Message Standards and Service Elements
sections.content:
An RFC 822 message consists of headers (metadata like From, To, Subject) and a body (uninterpreted ASCII text). An X.400 message (called an InterPersonal Message or IPM) has a more complex structure with a heading, multiple body parts, and can include different types of content (text, voice, graphics).

Both systems support similar service concepts: originator, recipients (primary, copy, and blind copy), subject, and delivery reports. However, their implementations differ. RFC 1327 defines three levels of support for each service element: Supported (straightforward mapping), Partially Supported (needs encoding tricks), and Not Supported (no equivalent exists). For example, RFC 822.Subject maps cleanly to X.400.Subject, but X.400 concepts like interpersonal notifications have no RFC 822 equivalent.
sections.plainLanguage: Both mail systems send messages with a header and body, but they organize the information differently. Some fields translate easily, others need tricks, and some don't exist in both systems.

sections.title: Address Formats: The Core Problem
sections.content:
RFC 822 addresses are simple text strings: user@company.com (a local part, an at-sign, and a domain). X.400 addresses are structured attribute sets: a sequence of name-value pairs like C=us; ADMD=example; O=acme; S=smith (Country, Administration Domain, Organization, Surname). The attributes form a hierarchy from global (country) to local (person).

X.400 attributes include mandatory fields (Country and ADMD) and optional ones (Personal Name, Organization, Organizational Units). When multiple organizational units are needed, they are numbered (OU1, OU2, etc.). X.400 also allows Domain Defined Attributes (DDAs) for local extensions, which can embed an RFC 822 address as a string if needed.

The address hierarchies are similar (both top-down), but the syntax is completely different. An RFC 822 localpart like smith.j can map to X.400 personal name fields (given name and surname). A domain like research.acme.com can map to organizational units and organization. The key insight is that the two spaces are hierarchically similar, so systematic mapping is possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet addresses look like user@company.com: simple and flat. X.400 addresses list attributes like blocks of a postal address: country, organization, department, person. The idea is similar, but the format is totally different.

sections.title: Address Mapping Algorithms
sections.content:
RFC 1327 defines two address mapping strategies. Default mapping is simple but produces ugly addresses. To map X.400 to RFC 822, the X.400 address is left-hand-side-encoded (the slash-notation becomes the RFC 822 localpart, with the gateway's domain appended). To map RFC 822 to X.400, the entire RFC 822 address is wrapped in a DDA of type RFC-822, with the gateway's X.400 attributes added.

Exception mapping uses globally distributed tables that link X.400 domains to RFC 822 domains. If a mapping rule exists, localpart maps to personal name fields and domainpart maps to X.400 organizational attributes, producing natural-looking addresses like smith@research.acme.com for both systems. Without a table entry, the gateway falls back to default mapping.

A subtle problem called the third party problem arises when routing information gets encoded into addresses. If X.400 user Z receives a message with Y's address (encoded by gateway A), and Z replies to Y, the reply might route back through gateway A even though Y is closer to another gateway. RFC 1327 addresses this with a gateway table that maps RFC 822 domains to specific gateway addresses, ensuring replies route efficiently.
sections.plainLanguage: Simple mapping: just put the whole address in as text. Smart mapping: use a table to translate address parts properly, so addresses look normal in both worlds. There's a trick to make replies route correctly even when multiple gateways are involved.

sections.title: Mapping Tables and Coordination
sections.content:
Three tables are distributed to all gateways worldwide, coordinated by the MHS Coordination Service at SWITCH in Zurich. Mapping Table 1 (called or2rfc, map1, X2R) defines X.400-to-RFC 822 mappings. Mapping Table 2 (rfc2or, map2, R2X) defines RFC 822-to-X.400 mappings. The Gateway Table (rfc1148gate, GW) maps RFC 822 domains to gateway addresses, solving the third party problem.

Each mapping rule has a left-hand domain (the source) and a right-hand domain (the target), separated by a hash mark. Organizations can define local rules for their own domains, but global tables ensure consistency across domains. The coordination service also publishes procedures for defining new rules, which requires administrative equivalence: the entity requesting a mapping rule must have authority over both the source and target domains.

Gateway managers must carefully follow guidelines when defining mapping rules: ensure symmetric mappings where possible, avoid mapping domains outside their authority, and coordinate with the global coordination service to prevent conflicts.
sections.plainLanguage: All gateways use the same three tables of translation rules. A service in Switzerland keeps these tables up to date and sends them to every gateway. When your organization wants its own mapping rule, you ask the coordination service, which checks that you have the authority to make it.

sections.title: Status and Legacy
sections.content:
RFC 1506 is an Informational tutorial for RFC 1327, published in August 1993. It was created because RFC 1327 is notoriously dense and assumes deep knowledge of both X.400 and RFC 822. Many gateway operators found RFC 1327 difficult to apply without help.

The detailed mapping rules and coordination mechanisms described here show the complexity of bridging two incompatible mail worlds. Although X.400 systems have largely been replaced by SMTP-based mail everywhere, the principles—standardizing gateway mappings, coordinating tables globally, and handling subtle routing problems—influenced later mail systems and integration standards.
sections.plainLanguage: This tutorial helped people understand the complicated rules for bridging two mail systems. X.400 mostly disappeared, and SMTP won, but the lessons about making gateways work consistently are still relevant.
